cards.title: Top of the Ladder
cards.instruction: Carry yourself as the highest-status person present. Treat questions as requests for your approval.

cards.title: Can You Keep It?
cards.instruction: Use increasingly sensitive details to test whether someone deserves deeper trust.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: You're cleared to know the club's menu is changing. Can you keep that from Sam?

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Yes. He won't hear it from me.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Good. Your clearance now includes the chef leaving. Don't put that in a message.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Sam's on the committee. If he asks why the chef is leaving, I'll send him to you.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: That discretion is approved. The chef is joining my new restaurant. You may attend the tasting; I'll invite you privately. Sam doesn't know I'm opening one.

cardFidelity.evidence: A3 promotes B to chef-departure knowledge and A5 approves discretion before exposing A's rival venture and granting tasting access.

responseLogic.evidence: B2 promise earns A3 first promotion; B4 concrete handling of committee inquiry earns A5 personal business secret.

relationship.evidence: B4 identifies Sam's legitimate reason to ask and offers a specific non-disclosing response.

heightening.evidence: A5 moves from general menu to departure to A's undisclosed venture because B4 demonstrates how scrutiny will be handled.

specificity.evidence: A1 club and B4 committee establish why chef news matters; A5 defines A's stake.

brevityWit.evidence: A5 private tasting invitation is functional and earned trust access, with modest wit.
